questions.text: Enthalpy is defined as:
questions.detailed: $H \equiv U + PV$. The $PV$ term is the "room-making" work; adding it to $U$ converts a constant-volume heat into a constant-pressure heat, so that at constant $P$, $q=\Delta H$.

questions.text: The heat measured at constant pressure with only $PV$ work equals:
questions.detailed: At constant pressure $q_p = \Delta H$. (At constant volume, $q_v=\Delta U$.) This is precisely why enthalpy is the natural energy function for open, atmospheric-pressure processes such as metallurgical reactions.

questions.text: An exothermic reaction has:
questions.detailed: Exothermic means heat is released by the system, so enthalpy decreases: $\Delta H<0$. Endothermic reactions absorb heat and have $\Delta H>0$.

questions.text: For an ideal gas, $C_P - C_V$ is equal to:
questions.detailed: Because $H=U+PV=U+nRT$, differentiating gives $C_P-C_V=nR$, or $C_P-C_V=R$ per mole. At constant pressure the gas must also do expansion work $P\Delta V=R\Delta T$ per mole, so more heat is needed for the same $\Delta T$.

questions.text: The fundamental reason $C_P > C_V$ for a gas is:

options.label: b
options.text: At constant pressure part of the heat supplied goes into expansion work rather than raising temperature

options.label: d
options.text: Enthalpy is not a state function

questions.detailed: When heated at constant pressure the gas expands, doing work $P\Delta V$ on the surroundings. That portion of the heat does not raise $T$, so a larger $q$ (hence larger $C_P$) is needed to achieve the same $\Delta T$ as at constant volume.

questions.text: Kirchhoff's equation expresses:

options.label: b
options.text: How reaction enthalpy varies with temperature: $d(\Delta H)/dT = \Delta C_P$

options.label: d
options.text: The entropy of a phase transition

questions.detailed: Kirchhoff's equation: $\dfrac{d(\Delta H)}{dT}=\Delta C_P$, where $\Delta C_P=\sum C_P(\text{products})-\sum C_P(\text{reactants})$. Integrating from $T_1$ to $T_2$ gives $\Delta H_{T_2}=\Delta H_{T_1}+\int \Delta C_P\,dT$.

questions.text: The molar heat capacity of a substance is constant at $25\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$. The enthalpy change on heating $2$ mol from $300\ \mathrm{K}$ to $350\ \mathrm{K}$ is:
questions.detailed: $\Delta H = nC_P\Delta T = 2\times25\times50 = 2500\ \mathrm{J}$. With constant $C_P$ the integral is simply $nC_P\Delta T$.

questions.text: The standard enthalpy of formation of a compound is the enthalpy change when:

options.label: a
options.text: One mole of it is burnt completely in oxygen

options.label: b
options.text: One mole of it is formed from its constituent elements in their standard states

options.label: c
options.text: One mole of it is dissolved in water

questions.detailed: $\Delta H_f^\circ$ refers to forming *one mole* of the compound from its elements in their most stable standard states. By convention $\Delta H_f^\circ=0$ for an element in its standard state.

questions.text: "The standard enthalpy of formation of $\mathrm{O_2(g)}$ is zero."
questions.detailed: True. $\mathrm{O_2(g)}$ is the standard-state form of the element oxygen, so its $\Delta H_f^\circ$ is defined as zero. (Contrast with entropy, where $S^\circ\neq0$ even for elements.)

questions.text: For a reaction in which $\Delta n_{\text{gas}}=-2$ at $298\ \mathrm{K}$, the relation between $\Delta H$ and $\Delta U$ is:
questions.detailed: For ideal gases $\Delta H=\Delta U+\Delta n_{\text{gas}}RT$. With $\Delta n_{\text{gas}}=-2$, this becomes $\Delta H=\Delta U-2RT$. Gas molecules are consumed, so the system's $PV$ term drops.

questions.text: For a monatomic ideal gas, the values of $C_V$, $C_P$ and $\gamma=C_P/C_V$ are:
questions.detailed: A monatomic gas has only translational energy: $C_V=\tfrac32R$, so $C_P=C_V+R=\tfrac52R$ and $\gamma=\tfrac{5/2}{3/2}=\tfrac53\approx1.67$.

questions.text: Which statements about enthalpy are correct?

statements.text: $H$ is a state function and is extensive.
For an ideal gas, $H$ depends only on $T$.
$\Delta H = q$ for any process regardless of conditions.

questions.detailed: I and II are true. III is false: $\Delta H=q$ only for constant-pressure processes with no non-$PV$ work. Enthalpy is a state function, so $\Delta H$ is well-defined for any process, but it equals $q$ only under those conditions.

questions.text: $C_P$ of a substance is given as $C_P=a+bT$. Integrating $\int C_P\,dT$ from $T_1$ to $T_2$ gives the enthalpy change as:
questions.detailed: $\int_{T_1}^{T_2}(a+bT)\,dT=a(T_2-T_1)+\tfrac{b}{2}(T_2^2-T_1^2)$. This is the Kirchhoff integration for a linear $C_P$.

questions.text: When a phase change (melting/boiling) occurs between $T_1$ and $T_2$, Kirchhoff's integration must be modified by:

options.label: b
options.text: Adding the latent heat at the transition temperature and switching to the new phase's $C_P$

questions.detailed: You cannot integrate $C_P$ straight across a transition. Stop exactly at the transition temperature, add $\Delta H_{\text{trans}}$, then continue with the heat capacity of the new phase. Skipping the latent heat is a very common error.

questions.text: Choose the correct option:
questions.reason: Enthalpy is a state function, so a quantity is independent of the path between the same initial and final states.

options.label: a
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: b
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: c
options.text: A is true but R is false

options.label: d
options.text: A is false but R is true

questions.detailed: solid → gas (sublimation) can be reached either directly or via solid → liquid → gas. Because $H$ is a state function (R), the two routes must give the same total, giving the equality (A). This is a mini application of Hess's Law.

questions.text: "The enthalpy change for condensation of a vapour is positive."
questions.detailed: False. Condensation is the reverse of vaporisation; since vaporisation is endothermic ($\Delta H_{\text{vap}}>0$), condensation is exothermic with $\Delta H=-\Delta H_{\text{vap}}<0$.

questions.text: The Joule–Thomson coefficient $\mu_{JT}=(\partial T/\partial P)_H$ equals zero for:

options.label: c
options.text: A van der Waals gas at all conditions

questions.detailed: Joule–Thomson expansion is isenthalpic. For an ideal gas $H=H(T)$ only, so at fixed $H$ the temperature cannot change: $\mu_{JT}=0$. Real gases show either cooling or heating depending on conditions.

questions.text: The standard enthalpy of combustion is the enthalpy change when:

options.label: a
options.text: One mole of a substance is formed

options.label: b
options.text: One mole of a substance is completely burnt in oxygen

options.label: c
options.text: One mole of a substance dissolves

questions.detailed: Combustion enthalpy refers to fully burning one mole of the substance in excess oxygen, with all elements ending as their most stable oxides (e.g. C→CO₂, H→H₂O). It is always negative for combustible fuels.

questions.text: If $C_P - C_V = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$ for a gas, the gas is:

options.label: c
options.text: A solid at its melting point

questions.detailed: $C_P-C_V=nR$; per mole this is $R=8.314\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, the ideal-gas value. Real gases at high pressure deviate from this.

questions.text: Which of the following statements best explains why enthalpy (rather than internal energy) is used for open, flow processes at atmospheric pressure?

options.label: a
options.text: Enthalpy excludes the $PV$ "flow" work automatically, so heat effects appear directly

options.label: b
options.text: Enthalpy is easier to measure than internal energy

questions.detailed: In a steady-flow process the surroundings do $PV$ "flow work" on the incoming fluid. Adding this to $U$ gives $H=U+PV$, so the energy balance at constant pressure involves only $H$, and measured heat effects map directly onto $\Delta H$.
